title: Producing algorithms: flowcharts
starter: Draw a diagram showing how you decide what to wear each morning. Where does your diagram branch?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: The five symbols
facts: Rounded box: start or stop, called a terminal.
Rectangle: a process. Diamond: a decision. Double-sided box: a subprogram.
stations.challenge: Draw all five symbols and label what each one is for.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Rounded box: start or stop, called a terminal.
Also credit: Parallelogram: input or output.

questions.q: Match each flowchart symbol to what it represents.
questions.a: Rounded box → Start or stop; Parallelogram → Input or output; Rectangle → A process; Diamond → A decision

questions.q: Which symbol has two arrows leaving it?
questions.a: The diamond, because a decision has a yes path and a no path

stations.name: Reading a flowchart
facts: Start at the terminal marked Start and follow the arrows.
At a diamond, read the condition and take the yes or no path.
Stop when you reach the terminal marked Stop.
stations.challenge: Follow a flowchart by hand with an input of 7 and record the output.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Start at the terminal marked Start and follow the arrows.
Also credit: At a diamond, read the condition and take the yes or no path.

questions.q: A flowchart reads: input n, is n greater than 10, if yes output 'big', if no output 'small'. What does an input of 7 produce?
A flowchart has an arrow going back to an earlier box. What does that show?

stations.name: Decisions
facts: A diamond holds a condition that is either true or false.
Label the two arrows leaving it, usually Yes and No.
Nested decisions let a flowchart pick between more than two outcomes.
stations.challenge: Draw a flowchart that reports pass, merit or distinction from a mark.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A diamond holds a condition that is either true or false.
Also credit: Label the two arrows leaving it, usually Yes and No.

questions.q: Put these boxes into the order a grading flowchart would use.
questions.a: Start → Input the mark → Is the mark 70 or more? → Is the mark 50 or more? → Output the grade → Stop

questions.q: Why must the highest grade be tested first?
questions.a: Otherwise a mark of 80 would match the lower condition and be given the wrong grade

stations.name: Loops in flowcharts
facts: A loop is drawn as an arrow back to an earlier point.
A condition decides whether to go round again or carry on.
Without a way out, the flowchart describes a program that never stops.
stations.challenge: Draw a flowchart that adds up ten numbers entered by the user.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A loop is drawn as an arrow back to an earlier point.
Also credit: A condition decides whether to go round again or carry on.

questions.q: Put these boxes into the order for a flowchart that totals ten numbers.
questions.a: Start → Set the total to 0 and the count to 0 → Input a number → Add it to the total and add 1 to the count → Is the count 10? → Output the total → Stop

questions.q: What happens if the loop's decision can never be true?
questions.a: The program never stops: an infinite loop

stations.name: Flowchart or pseudocode?
facts: Flowcharts show the shape of an algorithm, which suits explaining it to someone else.
They get unwieldy for long algorithms, where pseudocode is clearer.
Both describe the same thing; the exam may ask for either.
stations.challenge: Give one advantage of a flowchart and one of pseudocode.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Flowcharts show the shape of an algorithm, which suits explaining it to someone else.
Also credit: They get unwieldy for long algorithms, where pseudocode is clearer.

questions.q: When is a flowchart the better choice?
questions.a: When explaining the shape of an algorithm to someone who does not program
A flowchart and pseudocode can describe exactly the same algorithm

stations.name: Drawing a flowchart in the exam
facts: Use the right shape for each kind of step: marks are lost for a rectangle where a diamond belongs.
Label both arrows leaving a decision.
Start and stop with terminals, and check every path reaches a stop.
stations.challenge: Draw a flowchart for a login system that allows three attempts.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Use the right shape for each kind of step: marks are lost for a rectangle where a diamond belongs.
Also credit: Label both arrows leaving a decision.

questions.q: Which of these would lose marks in a flowchart question? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Using a rectangle for a decision; Leaving the arrows from a diamond unlabelled; A path that never reaches a stop

questions.q: A flowchart's decision has only one arrow leaving it. What is wrong?
questions.a: A decision must have both a true and a false path

final.name: Final challenge: build the flowchart

questions.q: Put the boxes of the ticket machine flowchart into order.
questions.a: Start → Input the passenger's age → Is the age under 16? → Set the price to £2 or £4 → Output the price → Stop

questions.q: Which flowchart symbol would each step use?
questions.a: Start = Terminal; Stop = Terminal; Input the age = Input/output; Output the price = Input/output; Set the price to £2 = Process; Is the age under 16? = Decision

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: State what the diamond symbol represents in a flowchart.
points: At a diamond, read the condition and take the yes or no path.
A diamond holds a condition that is either true or false.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark for a correct answer.

exam.q: Explain why a decision symbol must have two arrows leaving it.
points: Label both arrows leaving a decision.
Label the two arrows leaving it, usually Yes and No.
Rectangle: a process. Diamond: a decision. Double-sided box: a subprogram.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: A cinema charges £5 for under-18s and £9 for everyone else. Draw a flowchart for a program that inputs an age and outputs the price.
points: Without a way out, the flowchart describes a program that never stops.
Nested decisions let a flowchart pick between more than two outcomes.
Flowcharts show the shape of an algorithm, which suits explaining it to someone else.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 6.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
